**WAPL** (105.7 FM) is a Mainstream rock formatted radio stationlicensed to Appleton, Wisconsin, that serves the Green Bay and Appleton-Oshkosh areas. The station is owned by Woodward Communications, and has studios on College Avenue in Appleton, with transmitting facilities located near the WGBA Tower west of unincorporated Shirley in the Town of Glenmore in southeastern Brown County.
WAPL radio made its on-air debut in 1952, operating on a frequency of 1570 AM under the ownership of the Bartell family. It was the third AM station in the market, but the first to serve the younger audience with rock and roll music.

**WAPL-FM**, operating on a frequency of 105.7 MHz, was added in 1965 when an FM antenna was installed on the existing WAPL (AM) tower in Menasha. The initial power was around 20,000 watts at an antenna height of 160 feet. The station's format was beautiful music.
In 1965, WAPL-FM was upgraded to a 50,000-watt signal at 200 feet with a new tower on The Zuelke Building in downtown Appleton.
By 1977, having gone through a number of ownership and format changes, WAPL-FM changed its call letters to **WCXR** and briefly became a Christian station. This change lasted only eight months before changing format again, this time to album rock. Shortly thereafter, the station's call letters reverted to **WAPL-FM**. The on-air line up included Laura Morgan, Dan Adams and program director Steve Brown.
Studios
In 1978, WAPL AM and FM were offered for sale. WAPL-FM was purchased by Woodward Communications, Inc., of Dubuque, Iowa. Woodward already owned an AM station, WHBY, in the Appleton market. A strategy was developed to include the newly purchased station in the already planned new facility for WHBY on Appleton's southeast side. The plans included an upgrade of WAPL's signal to 100,000 watts of power and 450 feet of height for the antenna.
The new facilities were completed in the early fall of 1979, and WAPL and its new sister station, WHBY, won the Broadcast Management and Engineering award for "Best AM/FM Station" of 1979. Soon after the construction was complete, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ruled that high power FM station like WAPL should be at least 100,000 watts at 1000 feet. Immediately, the planning began for a new transmitter site which would allow WAPL to remain a Class C FM transmitting facility. During this time, most of the WAPL air staff went by only their first names and was composed of Robin, Dale, Cliff, Carl King, Laura Morgan, Mark Coulter and Operations Manager Dan Davis.

In October 1980, WAPL-FM began identifying itself as "The Rockin' Apple", under program director Wayne Shayne. WAPL would continue to use the nickname until 2002, at which time the station was re-branded as "Wisconsin's Rock Station". "The Rockin' Apple" was brought back as a station identifier in 2007 as preparations were being made for WAPL's 30th Anniversary celebration. In addition to Shayne, other members of the air staff during WAPL's history have included Rick Panneck, David Lee, Laura Morgan, Bob Baron, Rick Blades, and Nate Wright (Night Nate).
In April 1985, "The Mark and McNeal Morning Show" debuted with Mark Coulter, Rick McNeal and newsman Len Nelson. While Coulter departed after only eight months, McNeal and Nelson continued doing the morning show together until January 1999, when Nelson left the station to become news director of WGEE (now WTAQ) and was replaced by John Jordan. McNeal and Jordan would continue on the "Rockin' Apple Morning Show" until April 2002, when WAPL management dropped the show in favor of "Bob and Brian," a show originating from Milwaukee's WLZR (now WHQG). "Bob and Brian" aired on WAPL until March 2003. The syndicated show was a bust with Rockin' Apple listeners, causing WAPL to drop it in favor of a local, music-intensive morning shift. ("Bob and Brian" would eventually resurface in the Fox Cities radio market on WWWX.) In September 2003, WAPL reunited Rick McNeal and Len Nelson at their 25th Anniversary Celebration and announced that they would return to the station to once again helm the morning show.

WAPL received a construction permit August 27, 1987 to increase tower height and become a full Class C FM, nearly eight years after applying for it. The new transmitting facility was completed southeast of Green Bay in rural Shirley at a height of 1,175 feet above average terrain near WGBA-TV's transmitter, making the station "The 100,000 Watt Blowtorch of the Midwest". The station can be heard as far west from towns west of Wausau, as far east as cities across Lake Michigan such as Ludington and as far north as Iron Mountain, MI. The signal easily reaches the northern portions of the Milwaukee market, though a translator activated in 2015 broadcasting Milwaukee's AM sports station WSSP, also carried on 105.7, has removed some access to WAPL in that market.
The Rockin' Apple celebrated its 30th anniversary in 2008. WAPL was recognized by the American Red Cross in 2002 as Outstanding Media Partner for their fund raising efforts following the September 11 attacks in 2001. In addition to being a national Marconi Award finalist in 2006, WAPL has won numerous Wisconsin Area Music Industry Awards and was nominated for 2008 Station of the Year. WAPL remains radio-active in the community through charitable campaigns such as Rock Against Hunger, Rock For Kids, and Rock For The Cure. They partner annually with the Leukemia-Lymphoma Society, American Cancer Society, Children's Hospital, Paul's Pantry, and area domestic abuse shelters in raising nearly a million dollars for local charities. The current WAPL line-up includes The Rick and Cutter Show with news anchor Erin Davisson, The Liquid Lunch with Ross Maxwell, The Afternoon Road Show with Elwood and John Jordan, Andy Gardner, Home Brewed, House of Hair with Dee Snider, Nights with Alice Cooper, and Sammy Hagar's Top Rock Countdown.

**Appleton** (Menominee: _Ahkōnemeh_) is a city in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. It is the county seat of Outagamie County, with small portions extending into Calumet and Winnebago counties. Located on the Fox River north of Lake Winnebago, it is 30 miles (48 km) southwest of Green Bay and 100 miles (160 km) north of Milwaukee. The city had a population of 75,644 at the 2020 census, making it the sixth-most populous city in Wisconsin. The Appleton metropolitan statistical area had 243,147 residents. Appleton is part of the broader Fox Cities region.
Appleton was founded in the mid-19th century and developed as an industrial and educational center; Lawrence University was established in 1847. Its economy was historically based on paper manufacturing and has since expanded to include retail and healthcare sectors, with major facilities including St. Elizabeth Hospital and ThedaCare Regional Medical Center–Appleton. The city serves as a cultural center for the Fox River Valley, home to the Fox Cities Performing Arts Center and the History Museum at the Castle, which features exhibits on local history and notable residents such as magician Harry Houdini. It also hosts regional events such as Octoberfest[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10) and the Mile of Music.

### Native American history
[edit]
Appleton, Wisconsin – 1867[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)
The territory where Appleton is today was formerly occupied by the Ho-Chunk and the Menominee. The Menominee Nation ceded the territory to the United States in the Treaty of the Cedars in 1836.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-12) In the Menominee language, Appleton is known as _Ahkōnemeh_, or "watches for them place", while in Oneida it is known as _twaˀsʌ́thaˀ_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-14)
The first European settlers in Appleton were fur traders seeking to do business with Fox River Valley Native Americans. Hippolyte Grignon built the White Heron in 1835 to house his family and serve as an inn and trading post.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-timeline-15)

**Appleton** (Menominee: _Ahkōnemeh_) is a city in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. It is the county seat of Outagamie County, with small portions extending into Calumet and Winnebago counties. Located on the Fox River north of Lake Winnebago, it is 30 miles (48 km) southwest of Green Bay and 100 miles (160 km) north of Milwaukee. The city had a population of 75,644 at the 2020 census, making it the sixth-most populous city in Wisconsin. The Appleton metropolitan statistical area had 243,147 residents. Appleton is part of the broader Fox Cities region.
Appleton was founded in the mid-19th century and developed as an industrial and educational center; Lawrence University was established in 1847. Its economy was historically based on paper manufacturing and has since expanded to include retail and healthcare sectors, with major facilities including St. Elizabeth Hospital and ThedaCare Regional Medical Center–Appleton. The city serves as a cultural center for the Fox River Valley, home to the Fox Cities Performing Arts Center and the History Museum at the Castle, which features exhibits on local history and notable residents such as magician Harry Houdini. It also hosts regional events such as Octoberfest[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10) and the Mile of Music.

### Native American history
[edit]
Appleton, Wisconsin – 1867[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)
The territory where Appleton is today was formerly occupied by the Ho-Chunk and the Menominee. The Menominee Nation ceded the territory to the United States in the Treaty of the Cedars in 1836.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-12) In the Menominee language, Appleton is known as _Ahkōnemeh_, or "watches for them place", while in Oneida it is known as _twaˀsʌ́thaˀ_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-14)
The first European settlers in Appleton were fur traders seeking to do business with Fox River Valley Native Americans. Hippolyte Grignon built the White Heron in 1835 to house his family and serve as an inn and trading post.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin#cite_note-timeline-15)

**Outagamie County** ( _OW-tə-GAY-mee_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-1) is a county in the Fox Cities region of the U.S. state of Wisconsin, in the northeast of the state. As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

Outagamie County's government consists of an elected County Board of Supervisors, a County Executive, and 36 county agencies and departments.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-9)

Department heads are appointed by the county executive, subject to the approval of the board of supervisors. The county executive also appoints members to the county's boards and commissions. ## Fox Cities at the Center.
Outagamie County sits at the heart of the Fox Cities region, anchored by Appleton and extending through a mix of smaller cities, villages, and townships that together define one of the more economically active corridors in Wisconsin. The Fox River runs through the county from south to north, and the industrial and commercial history built along that waterway has left a legacy of stable employment, established neighborhoods, and a regional identity tied to manufacturing, paper, and professional services.
Appleton anchors the county as its largest city and economic hub, but Outagamie County's strength comes from the range of communities surrounding it. Kaukauna, Kimberly, Freedom, Seymour, and Wrightstown each bring their own school districts, character, and price points to the market, giving buyers genuine options across a spectrum from urban walkability to rural acreage. The Fox Cities metro area, which spans Outagamie, Calumet, and Winnebago counties, consistently ranks among the stronger small metro economies in the Midwest.
Housing in Outagamie County covers significant ground. Buyers in Appleton find an urban market with strong demand and limited inventory. Buyers in the county's smaller communities find more space, independent school districts, and price points that reflect the township rather than the city. The county's location between Green Bay to the north and the broader Milwaukee corridor to the south keeps it connected to two major labor markets while maintaining its own economic weight.

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

# Outagamie County
## Fox Cities at the Center.
Outagamie County sits at the heart of the Fox Cities region, anchored by Appleton and extending through a mix of smaller cities, villages, and townships that together define one of the more economically active corridors in Wisconsin. The Fox River runs through the county from south to north, and the industrial and commercial history built along that waterway has left a legacy of stable employment, established neighborhoods, and a regional identity tied to manufacturing, paper, and professional services.
Appleton anchors the county as its largest city and economic hub, but Outagamie County's strength comes from the range of communities surrounding it. Kaukauna, Kimberly, Freedom, Seymour, and Wrightstown each bring their own school districts, character, and price points to the market, giving buyers genuine options across a spectrum from urban walkability to rural acreage. The Fox Cities metro area, which spans Outagamie, Calumet, and Winnebago counties, consistently ranks among the stronger small metro economies in the Midwest.
Housing in Outagamie County covers significant ground. Buyers in Appleton find an urban market with strong demand and limited inventory. Buyers in the county's smaller communities find more space, independent school districts, and price points that reflect the township rather than the city. The county's location between Green Bay to the north and the broader Milwaukee corridor to the south keeps it connected to two major labor markets while maintaining its own economic weight.

Green Bay, center, is the seat of Brown County. The city of Oconto (half cut off at the bottom right) is the county seat of Oconto County. Slightly above and much further right of Oconto is Oconto Falls, also in Oconto County. The somewhat larger city above Oconto Falls is Pulaski, which is in Brown County at the very border with Shawano County. Shawano County extends between Pulaski and past the edge of the photograph.
The large city in the top right is Appleton, the county seat of Outagamie County. To the left of Appleton and across the northern edge of Lake Winnebago is Brillion in Calumet County.
The village directly to the left of Green Bay and its immediate suburbs is Denmark, in Brown County. The smaller communities above and slightly to the left of Denmark (including Cooperstown, Maribel, and Kellnersville) are in Manitowoc County.
Luxembourg (larger village in lower left) and Casco (half cut off at lower far left) are in Kewaunee County.
Brown County is rather conservative for an urban county. Since 1968, Brown County has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in all but two elections, 1996 and 2008. Democratic strength is concentrated in the city of Green Bay, while the suburban and rural areas typically vote Republican.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-31)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

### Political representation
*   the [1st Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 1st Assembly district") contains just the northeast corner of Brown County then stretches into Kewaunee and Door counties, and is represented by Republican Joel Kitchens.  
*   the [2nd Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Assembly district") contains the southern half of Brown County and the northern half of neighboring Manitowoc County along with a small portion of Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Shae Sortwell.  
*   the [4th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_4th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 4th Assembly district") contains the northern Brown County municipalities of Howard and Suamico, and extends north to eastern Oconto County, and is represented by Republican David Steffen.  
*   the [5th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_5th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 5th Assembly district") contains western Brown County and eastern Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Joy Goeben.  
*   the [6th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_6th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 6th Assembly district") contains the northwestern Brown County municipalities of Pittsfield and Pulaski, then a wide area of the counties to the west, and is represented by Republican Elijah Behnke.  
*   the [88th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_88th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 88th Assembly district") contains all of De Pere, Allouez, and Bellevue, and is represented by Republican Ben Franklin.  
*   the [89th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_89th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 89th Assembly district") contains all of Ashwaubenon and part of the western side of Green Bay, and is represented by Democrat Ryan Spaude.

Green Bay, center, is the seat of Brown County. The city of Oconto (half cut off at the bottom right) is the county seat of Oconto County. Slightly above and much further right of Oconto is Oconto Falls, also in Oconto County. The somewhat larger city above Oconto Falls is Pulaski, which is in Brown County at the very border with Shawano County. Shawano County extends between Pulaski and past the edge of the photograph.
The large city in the top right is Appleton, the county seat of Outagamie County. To the left of Appleton and across the northern edge of Lake Winnebago is Brillion in Calumet County.
The village directly to the left of Green Bay and its immediate suburbs is Denmark, in Brown County. The smaller communities above and slightly to the left of Denmark (including Cooperstown, Maribel, and Kellnersville) are in Manitowoc County.
Luxembourg (larger village in lower left) and Casco (half cut off at lower far left) are in Kewaunee County.
Brown County is rather conservative for an urban county. Since 1968, Brown County has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in all but two elections, 1996 and 2008. Democratic strength is concentrated in the city of Green Bay, while the suburban and rural areas typically vote Republican.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-31)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).
